title: What is Fair in University Admissions?
description: Around the world, more students than ever are seeking a university education. When admission is competitive, how does a society and its universities answer the question: who should get in? This question is complicated by the recognition of educational disparities in the primary and secondary systems that prepare students for university. Today, about a quarter of all countries have some sort of affirmative action programs - also known as reservations, quotas, or preferential admissions - and eligibility criteria range from race, caste, gender, ethnicity, and ruralness to educational and socioeconomic disadvantage. This course analyzes the development and impact of affirmative action policies within broader debates about equity and fairness in higher education. Case studies and guest speakers will be drawn from South Africa, Brazil, India, and the United States. Special focus will be given to South Africa, which first developed its policies under the country’s post-Apartheid Constitution. Site visits to higher education institutions in Cape Town and elsewhere will offer in-depth insights into the practical implications of these policies and the controversies that surround them.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
This is an Away course in South Africa

title: Multiple Identities, Multiple Inclusions?
description: How can governments and civil society organizations - including sports, arts, and cultural groups - enhance civic inclusion for marginalized communities? Political rights, public programs, and civic opportunities offer valuable material and symbolic benefits, yet many eligible individuals face barriers to access. These take-up gaps are often most pronounced among groups marginalized by gender, class, ability, age, race, or immigration status. This course explores how such disparities can be addressed by examining strategies that promote civic inclusion across multiple dimensions of exclusion. Through collaboration with local UAE and international organizations - such as sports clubs, religious institutions, cultural groups, and government agencies - students will investigate and assess existing and innovative approaches to reducing access gaps. Emphasis will be placed on identifying effective strategies to foster a more inclusive society.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Can Nature Save Us? The Politics of Climate Repair
description: This course examines how institutions and incentive-based mechanisms can protect and expand carbon-rich ecosystems - tropical forests and coastal "blue carbon" systems, such as mangroves - to address the climate crisis. Deforestation and mangrove destruction contribute significantly to global greenhouse gas emissions, while these ecosystems provide critical services for climate mitigation, biodiversity, and livelihoods. Despite multilateral frameworks such as REDD+ and emerging carbon credit markets, conservation efforts face a credibility crisis. Students will explore the global public goods nature of ecosystem protection, local incentives that drive ecosystem loss, climate finance and other strategies for promoting conservation and restoration, and methods for evaluating them. A unique feature of the course is a field visit to mangrove expansion and restoration projects in the UAE. Students will meet UAE-based experts to study blue carbon initiatives. Using insights from class and the field visits, students will develop team-based research projects that attempt to apply the lessons from the UAE's blue carbon experience to other contexts globally. The course draws on perspectives from economics, political science, international relations, conservation science, and anthropology, and emphasizes mixed-methods research and effective communication of findings.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Creative Robotics and Tech
description: What will the future of human and robot interaction look like? How can new technology and robots inspire human creativity and help us grow artistically? How can we use the intersection of art and tech to pursue research? Einstein said, “Play is the highest form of research.” By exploring technology through art and movement, how can we further research? How can this play out in the rapid development of both sectors in Abu Dhabi and the UAE? This course provides students the tools and knowledge to integrate robotics and new technology into their creative practice as artists and researchers (no prior experience required). Students will design and create a final project exploring the intersection between art and robotics and tech in various forms. Depending on the scale of the project, students will work together as one big group or smaller groups.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: International Peacebuilding and the Role of Education
description: This course explores the politics of conflict, peacebuilding, humanitarianism and the role of education in promoting violence or peace. We ask, what causes conflict and how is peace built? How do education, civil society, peacekeeping, and humanitarian aid factor in for both conflict and peace? What role do young people have in this process? Preliminary case studies include Afghanistan, Iran, Syria, Ukraine, and the US. We will meet with local and international organizations supporting peacebuilding (e.g., Human Rights Watch, IRC, UNHCR) as well as activists in exile. We will discuss sensitive topics related to social unrest and consider conflict-affected populations’ access to quality education during conflict or displacement, refugee migration, and peacebuilding. The class will take place in Athens, Greece, meet with displaced populations, and work in partnership with a local organization that trains refugee youth in media arts and migration reporting. Learning firsthand about refugee life, students will write and present a short research article based on data collected while in Greece.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
This is an Away course in Greece

title: Arts for Transformation: The Case of Cambodia
description: How can arts and culture drive transformation and healing in post-conflict societies? And how can they contribute to heritage preservation, historical narrative shaping, and contemporary expression in such settings? This course explores the role of the arts in reconstruction, revitalization, reconciliation and peacebuilding. We will examine the methods and tools that prove successful and consider why other approaches fail. Using Cambodia's complex history as a case study, we will investigate how shifting narratives, cultural governance, social welfare, and the cultural economy intersect to shape the arts ecosystem. Through meetings with local artists in Phnom Penh and Siem Reap; site visits from the World Heritage site of Angkor temple complex to the Tuol Sleng Genocide museum, students will gain insight into the social, cultural, economic, and political factors that shape and drive Cambodia's dynamic and transformative arts scene. This course will be taught in Cambodia and will count as an Away J-Term course.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
This is an Away course in Cambodia.

title: Gendering Islam in the Global City
description: Gendering Islam in the Global City: How do the physical spaces and neighborhoods of a city shape the way gender and religion interact? How do individuals embody, express, and live out the relationships between religion and gender? What types of citizens and subjects are produced by different configurations of space, religion, and gender? This course will examine these questions through the lens of Muslim societies across the Middle East and globe, analyzing how religion is molded by the state, capitalism, and other social institutions to produce gendered regimes and subjectivities. Students will read foundational theories on gender, religion, and embodiment as well as cutting-edge research on gender in contemporary Muslim societies, with a focus on urban environments. Comparing Muslim communities across time and space, we will ask the degree to which Islam can explain different configurations of public piety and moral governance. Through fieldwork in the urban landscapes of the UAE, students will observe how configurations of the “Islamic city” have evolved. We will visit mosques, community organizations and ethnic enclaves, examining how religion and gender interact in spaces of home, work, play and governance.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Reporting (on) Migration
description: How do journalists report on migration, and how does that reporting influence public debate and policy? How does reporting on displaced populations shape the migrant experience itself, and what ethical responsibilities do journalists have when reporting on vulnerable communities? This course examines two comparative case studies as they play out in Greece and beyond, focusing on the Syrian refugee situation of 2015 and the displacement of Ukrainians following Russia's 2022 invasion. Students will work with Refocus Media Labs, an organization that trains refugee journalists, to examine firsthand the practical and ethical challenges of migration reporting. We will also engage with academic literature alongside long-form journalism and learn to critically analyze news coverage and evaluate how race, geopolitics, language, and visual storytelling shape public perception and political response. Coursework includes daily reading quizzes, regular reporting and editing exercises, and a final reported feature on migration grounded in field research and interviews.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
This is an Away course in Greece.

title: Beyond Bigness: The Everyday City
description: How is one to evaluate which urban design ideology to subscribe to, and thus design better environments? What are the different urban design ideals informing the design of cities? How can urban design facilitate everyday encounters? These questions underscore Jane Jacobs' warning of a global "dark age" in community life. Our neighborhoods are experiencing a collapse in everyday social interactions. Planners and designers criticize the excessive over-scaled urbanism seen in post-1990s developments, characterized by grand designs, fragmentation, vast expanses of glass and metal, and a loss of spontaneity within cities. In contrast to the traditional neighborhoods of the pre-1990s era, many new developments lack simplicity and dense physical layouts, which hampers neighborliness. To address this decline, it is essential to understand what enables everyday urbanism and good city forms. The course draws on unobtrusive observations of hidden sites to explore everydayness in Abu Dhabi and Dubai. The course materials and engagement with sites are structured to unravel the complexities of urban design and promote vibrant communities.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Practicing Politics and Government in an Age of Disruption
description: What drives global disruption, and how must leaders adapt traditional tools - diplomacy, defense, and communications - to an age of populism and technological upheaval? The first quarter of the 21st century has been defined by rapid, seismic events: 9/11 (2001), the Iraq War (2003), the 2008 financial crisis, the Syrian conflict (2011), Russia’s invasions of Ukraine (2014, 2022), the COVID-19 pandemic (2020), and renewed Middle East tensions. Together, these crises have fueled international insecurity and domestic populism. In this course, students will investigate the causes and consequences of this turbulence, focusing on the choices confronting world leaders. Drawing on original source material, political commentary, and the instructor’s real-world expertise, students will examine how leadership tools are evolving. Students will interview expert witnesses - including advisors, civil servants, politicians, and journalists. Each topic concludes with a practical writing exercise where students apply these insights to navigate the choices leaders face in a disrupted world.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: The Age of New Nationalisms
description: In what ways does the resurgence of nationalism in the 21st century signify a new age, and how is this shaping global political dynamics, cultural identities, economic policies, and international relations? This course introduces students to the nature, causes and policy implications of these new nationalisms. It combines data analysis, including text as data methods, with a body of interdisciplinary readings, examples from the MENA region, South Asia, European and the U.S, and field visits to monuments and museums in the U.A.E. to help us distinguish between different types of nationalism. Students will learn how to construct concepts and typologies of nationalism, link these to data, generate original measures and use these measures to map the trends, cause and consequences of contemporary nationalisms.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Why It Stays the Same: Global Perspectives on Inequality
description: Why is inequality such a common and persistent characteristic across drastically different societies – even when countries themselves change so often? We will approach this question from both theoretical and empirical perspectives to better understand inequalities across multiple lenses. A particular focus will be placed on inequality in China and the US, with examples from many other contexts. Through site visits to migrant schools, community-based organizations, and cultural centers and meetings with local experts in Shanghai, students will learn to compare, contrast, and analyze different forms of inequality and inequities critically. Ultimately, students will become better ‘understanders’ of their own social worlds.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
This is an away course in Shanghai

title: Ethnography and Experience
description: How do we understand social life in an unfamiliar city - and what happens when that city turns out to be more familiar than we expected? This course takes students to Florence for an immersive experience in ethnographic fieldwork. Ethnography emphasizes firsthand observation to interpret social life by standing in others’ shoes - but it also asks us to examine where we stand ourselves. Students will practice observation, interviewing, and note-taking in diverse settings: markets, piazzas, cafés, luxury shopping streets, and immigrant communities. Florence offers rich possibilities: a Renaissance heritage city shaped by global tourism and contemporary migration, where students may find themselves observing spaces where their own communities gather. We will grapple with core concepts - reflexivity, variation, the ethnographic fallacy, standpoint theory - and pay special attention to the ethics of representing others in writing. Through fieldwork and a final paper, students will connect observations to larger forces: labor markets, migration, citizenship, the performance of status, and tourism’s transformation of urban space.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
Class Times are shown in the Florence, Italy time zone. Make sure you convert to your local time zone, if needed.
This is an Away course in Florence

title: Language, Religion, and Ethnicity
description: What is language? Where is language? What are religion and ethnicity? What is the connection between them? The seminar offers a linguistic view of religion and ethnicity and looks into the sociolinguistic history, society, and culture of the US and the Arab world. We will consider the great diversity of communicative systems we encounter as a source of enrichment for individuals and the nation. We will also study the universal phenomenon of language change and how it affects our understanding of language behavior religiously and ethnically. Students will explore core concepts of linguistics with an emphasis on descriptive linguistics and sociolinguistics. Students will employ sociolinguistic methods to examine the relationship between language and ethnicity, language and nationalism, language and power, language and religion, language and gender, language and space, and language and education. We will explore some pockets of language use in the UAE (such as the Shiḥḥi tribe in RAK) as an opportunity to conduct field study, using the IPA (International Phonetic Alphabet),sociolinguistic interviews, and the method of Linguistic Landscape.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Law in Entrepreneurship
description: How do law and contracts shape innovation and entrepreneurial success? Can legal strategy become a source of competitive advantage rather than simply managing risk? Law in Entrepreneurship examines the legal foundations of building and scaling successful startups. The course explores how law and contracts shape entrepreneurial strategy, demonstrating that legal principles not only manage risk but also create value and competitive advantage. Students gain practical knowledge of entity formation, founder agreements, intellectual property, financing, employment, compliance, and exit strategies while developing an understanding of the legal challenges facing founders, investors, and executives. Through case studies and real world applications, students act as entrepreneurs and strategic advisors, solving legal and business problems that drive growth, operations, and investment readiness. The course emphasizes using legal strategy to protect innovation, structure relationships, allocate risk, and support decision making. Students leave with the legal fluency needed to anticipate challenges and build ventures that are resilient, ethical, and positioned for long term success.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: The Global Bible
description: What makes a text authoritative? Why do some writings endure for millennia, shaping the beliefs, identities, and institutions of societies far removed from the worlds in which they were first composed? This course explores these questions through the global history of the Bible and is designed for students with or without prior knowledge of this text. Sacred to Jews and Christians, foundational to Islam, and deeply influential in modern literature, politics, philosophy, and law, the Bible is a truly global book and has acquired remarkably different meanings across cultures and historical periods. Through fieldwork in the UAE, including visits to religious communities, museums, and cultural institutions, students study how diverse groups and individuals transmit, receive, adapt, interpret, and transform the text to new social and cultural circumstances today. By bringing together history, religious studies, and experiential learning, the course explores how communities continually negotiate the authority of texts in changing social, political, and ethical worlds.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Environmental Governance
description: Human activities are having an unprecedented impact on the planet. Is it still possible to govern our way out of the most serious environmental threats facing humanity - or are we already beyond the point of control? This course examines how environmental crises are (or are not) being managed. Students will analyze the interplay between knowledge, policy formulation, and stakeholder roles – exploring how scientific uncertainty influences policy development, how responsibility for action is allocated, and the competing interests of actors ranging from businesses to indigenous groups. Fieldwork will enable students to experience the governance process firsthand: from the challenges of biodiversity protection with conservation managers at the Mangrove National Park, to the promise (or pitfalls) of new energy technologies with start-ups and multinationals at the World Future Energy Summit, to the nuances of national climate strategies with policymakers at the Ministry of Climate Change and the Environment. A final project will ask students to be environmental policy entrepreneurs: applying insights from class to make the case for a new governance approach to an environmental challenge.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Researching Peace
description: What is peace and how can we study it? This course investigates (1) what peace means to people around the world and key approaches to measuring it; and (2) the varied methods, opportunities, and challenges of researching peacebuilding. With an approach rooted in experiential learning, students critically engage with the concept of peace. Students get hands-on practice with research techniques by participating in an ongoing study that explores if, how, and to what effect community leaders and ordinary people use cultural spaces like food, arts, and sports to bring people and groups together across divides. Throughout the course, students will participate in field-based research exploring these ideas around Paris, learn how to collect and analyze quantitative and/or qualitative data, hone their abilities to ask and answer important global questions, and practice communicating scholarly work to effect positive social change.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
Class Times are shown in the Paris, France time zone. Make sure you convert to your local time zone, if needed.
This is an Away course in Paris

title: Philanthropy Today: How Organized Money Fuels Innovation, Institutions and Movements
description: Why do people give? What does philanthropy engender? Philanthropy is one of the most powerful sectors in the world, shaping health systems, arts and culture, higher education, human rights, and numerous other public and private institutions and goods in many countries. But to many, these influential institutions and donors, from Andrew Carnegie and John D. Rockefeller to George Soros and Bill Gates, and a growing number of newly philanthropic billionaires, seem opaque and often unaccountable. This course explores the ancient roots of philanthropy, the creation of foundations in the modern era, their social impact, and their local context, including the legal and tax regimes that give rise to them. It will also delve into emerging trends, debates, practices and controversies, illuminated by case studies, talks with philanthropic leaders, site visits and intensive, ongoing exercise that will enable students to identify an area of philanthropic interest and need, choose an organization, and design a process for making an actual grant. It is especially timely with the rise of an increasingly active and strategic philanthropic sector in the United Arab Emirates.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Paper Art: History & Practice
description: How does the production of a material influence the art forms developed from it? How does a material’s accessibility determine who its artisans are? How does a material’s affordability influence the traditions formed around it? This course addresses these questions through a practice-based focus on the materiality and production of paper and paper crafting as a global art form. Beginning with the invention of paper, the papercraft movement has traditions and roots on all continents that have been openly shared and handed down through generations. This course is divided into several subject areas: the history of paper and paper making, paper folding, paper cutting, paper engineering, paper automata, and contemporary DIY electronics, fabrication, and paper craft movements. It will also include field trips to local artist studios and paper mills. Each subject area has associated readings, hands-on exercises, and a final creative work that addresses the forms explored.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
This is an Away course in Shanghai

title: Can Art Save Lives? The Health Benefits of the Arts and Arts Therapies
description: In what ways can participating in the arts enhance mental, physical, social, civic, and public health? This course offers a dynamic, interdisciplinary exploration of how the arts and arts therapies are used in healthcare, cultural institutions, rehabilitation centers, schools, and communities to support health and wellbeing. Drawing on local examples of practice in Abu Dhabi and across the UAE, together with insights from advocates for the arts and wellbeing from other countries, students examine the transformative potential of the arts in supporting and improving lives in practice and policy. Through both individual and group creative activities in class and in the city, students will gain firsthand experience with the arts as a vital tool for fostering health, care, and well-being. Activities include arts-based activities in the class, lectures from local practitioners, and visits to cultural and health centers that have had a longstanding commitment to uniting the arts and wellbeing.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Make Art Here
description: Make Art Here: How does location provoke an art action? What about the locations we carry with us? Does the view out your window instigate how depth perception is represented in your work, or color palette? Offering a curated, immersive experience in art-making, woven inextricably with the city of Madrid, this course centers a consideration of Live Art, archival practices and publics as we encounter and invent contemporary art making practices in Spain’s capital. We will visit parks and gardens, performances, museums, neighborhoods of interest and arts institutions generating contemporary work across all mediums. Students may switch mediums between projects and are invited to explore time based art (music, performance, film etc.) as well as fine arts (painting, drawing, collage, etc.). Students enrolled in this class can expect to walk a great deal and to attend evening and morning events. This course will be taught at NYU Madrid and will count as an Away J-Term course.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
Class Times are shown in the Madrid, Spain time zone. Make sure you convert to your local time zone, if needed.
This is an Away course in Madrid.

title: Art Markets
description: What is the worth of art? How do market systems determine what counts as art and what cultural expressions endure? This class explores the production, sale, display and exchange of artworks, and the patrons, artists, curators, museums, banks and art fairs driving this economic, social and political form of cultural production and aesthetic valuation. While students learn about global artists and institutions, we begin with art markets in Europe in the 15th century and expand globally through case studies to the present day. Our investigation examines patterns of transportation, exchange and trade; artists’ materials and practices; interactions of collectors, critics, artists and curators; art fairs, auction houses, investment banks and commercial galleries; cultural districts and museum architecture; and cultural heritage theft and restitution. The course focuses on the emergence of contemporary art markets globally via trade routes, migration, cultural revolution, technological innovation, political conflict, energy markets and global competition. Special attention is paid to the Los Angeles arts ecosystem and its relation to the film and entertainment industry.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
Class Times are shown in the Los Angeles, CA, USA time zone. Make sure you convert to your local time zone, if needed.
This is an Away course in Los Angeles.

title: Dressing the Nation
description: What can national dress reveal about identity, belonging, and power? How is it shaped, preserved, or reimagined - and is it fashion or something else entirely? While centered on the Emirati National Dress, the course explores how national dress emerges, becomes standardized, and adapts to shifting urban, environmental, and social conditions. Special attention is given to the crafts that underpin Emirati dress - embroidery, weaving, scenting - and their cultural and symbolic significance across men’s and women’s attire. We also examine the contemporary economies of craft, from local artisanal practices to global fashion systems, considering how tradition is preserved, commodified, or reinterpreted - and the tensions that may arise, including appropriation, dilution, or loss of meaning. Through debates, design experiments, and fieldwork with local organizations, designers, and artisans, students will produce a final exhibition and develop a nuanced understanding of the evolving relationship between Emirati dress, craft, design, and fashion.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Guns, an American Story
description: Guns: An American Story: Firearms are the leading cause of death for children and teens in the U.S., and account for more than half of all suicides. In fact, the U.S. experiences significantly higher rates of gun violence than any other developed nation, including other high-income countries. What makes guns and gun violence a distinctly American story? In this course, we review the role of the Second Amendment and explore the root causes behind the country’s exceptionally high rates. We examine how local communities, including law enforcement and community-based organizations, are addressing the crisis, and evaluate the role of state and federal policies. Is gun violence primarily a public health crisis, a political crisis, a crime crisis, or all three? Drawing on current research, we assess evidence-based interventions and discuss what works. In-person meetings with practitioners and policymakers in New York City, including police, prosecutors, and community violence intervention organizations, help us gain a better understanding of the challenges and potential solutions to this urgent issue. Students will work in groups to develop proposed solutions to one specific type of gun violence.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
This is an Away course in New York

title: Saadiyat Studio
description: Can making be a form of thinking? What kinds of knowledge can only be generated in the studio? And how can the world itself function as an extended studio space? Saadiyat Studio is an intensive masterclass in studio-based research, open to students working in and across arts disciplines. It is a philosophy course with its sleeves rolled up: part artist residency, part writing retreat, part creative laboratory. The course posits that art rarely arrives fully formed. It takes shape through experimentation, drafts, trials, false starts, and unexpected turns. The studio is approached not only as a physical space, but as a mode of attention, a set of habits, and as a way of moving through the world. Rather than treating creative practice as executing ideas, it invites students to approach making as a way of generating knowledge. Students gain momentum on capstones or independent projects through sustained studio time, one-on-one mentoring, and the focus that comes from stepping outside daily academic routines. Alongside hands-on work, the course fosters reflection, peer exchange, and critical engagement with the UAE's arts community through field visits, guest lectures, and critiques.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: From Rags to K-pop: The Korean Human Resource Story
description: The Korean Human Resource Story: How did one of the poorest post-war nations transform into a leading economic and soft power, home to K-pop and K-dramas? This course explores the answer by focusing on South Korea’s most vital resource: its people. Through readings, videos, and an immersive learning experience in Seoul, students will gain a deep understanding of the relationship between a nation's people, culture, and progress. The course begins at the War Memorial of Korea to trace the nation's rise from post-war devastation. Corporate site visits and guest lectures will provide first-hand experience of early and current Korean HR policies, which fueled growth through labor-intensive manufacturing and exports, creating the powerful chaebols (family-controlled conglomerates). Students will assess how these principles were applied to the entertainment industry and culture, contributing to the rise of K-pop, through site visits and analyses of their favorite artists. Finally, the class will examine Korea’s plunging birth rate, a direct threat to its human resources. Students will interview local Koreans to discuss the social impact of K-pop and evaluate the generalizability of the K-pop model to their home culture.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
This is an Away course in South Korea.

title: Contemporary Geopolitics: Navigating Power, Alliances and Global Crises
description: Negotiation and Practice: Can global order survive when power, legitimacy, and justice diverge? This course explores the concepts, institutions, and dilemmas shaping contemporary global politics and treats diplomacy and multilateralism not as an academic abstraction but as a high-stakes political practice. Based in New York and drawing on engagements at the United Nations headquarters, diplomatic missions, and NGOs, students will examine how global power is negotiated and implemented in practice. Through lectures, practitioner-led discussions, and applied analysis, led by a past president of the UN, students will dissect the structural tensions between international justice, geopolitical stability, and the real distribution of power; examine when diplomacy yields to coercion, and practice the art of political translation. They will write and present a policy memo designed to convert complex historical contexts and systemic risk into actionable recommendations for decision-makers. The course’s experiential centerpiece is a rigorous simulation of an emergency UN Security Council session, testing students' empirical research, negotiation tactics, and rapid-fire decision-making.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
This is an Away course in New York.

title: The Mindful Brain: Current Neuroscience and Ancient Wisdom
description: How can we cultivate calm and focus in an age of constant digital stimulation? And how and why do various forms of mindfulness training impact mental health, wellbeing, and resilience? Traditionally, Western neuroscientific studies have investigated the mind from the “outside in”, seeking to quantify an objective truth about the nature of the mind, while centuries-old meditative practices explore the mind from the “inside out”. In this course, we explore our own minds through methods from both approaches. The course will begin from “the outside”, with discussions of assigned readings on meditation and on the neuroscientific study of brain states, culminating in measuring our brain activity and our cognitive abilities at the Neuroscience Center in Bangkok. We will then embark on a 5-6 day meditation practice retreat, visiting ancient temples and conversing with Buddhist monks about their experiences. We will again measure our cognitive performance and resting brain activity and will analyze this data to test our initial hypotheses about the influences of meditation on the brain. Finally, we will consider how to implement what we have learned in our daily lives.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
This is an Away course in Thailand.

title: Concrete: From Roman to 3D Printing
description: Concrete is the most consumed material on Earth after water, yet a major contributor to global CO2 emissions. Despite modern advancements in cement and concrete technologies, the remarkable durability of ancient Roman concrete - used in structures like the Pantheon and the Colosseum, which have lasted millennia - continues to outperform modern concrete. Can lessons from Roman concrete help us balance durability with the urgent need for sustainability in modern construction, including innovations such as 3D concrete printing? Through field visits in Rome to historic concrete sites and modern landmarks like the MAXXI Museum, along with hands-on work at one of Italy’s largest 3D concrete printing facilities, students will examine the engineering, environmental, and economic implications of concrete throughout its evolution. They will research contemporary efforts to create more sustainable alternatives, including recycled materials and low-carbon binders. For their final projects, students will reimagine concrete structures using 3D printing and other emerging technologies, analyzing their potential to reduce construction time, material waste, and carbon emissions.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
This is an Away course in Italy.

title: Shanghai Walks: Tracing the City’s Stories
description: Inspired by the rising trend of Chinese Citywalks - a social media phenomenon where young urbanites document slow-paced, observational walks through their cities - this course invites students to explore Shanghai on foot. We'll use the city as our classroom, asking how walking can help us better understand its complexity: what does a street-level view reveal about the city's histories, rapid changes, and the role of its residents in its story? Guided by local experts and lecturers, we'll complement our walks by studying theories of urban space and walking, Shanghai's colonial history, and its immigrant groups. As students gain a critical vocabulary for assessing urban issues, they will not only build a deeper understanding of Shanghai but also learn to apply these concepts to their own urban experiences. Students will document their walks through notes, photos, videos, and sound recordings, which will form the basis of a daily social media diary. Alongside an essay based on an interview with a city resident, this assignment is designed to sharpen students' observation and storytelling skills, helping them see how individual stories form the very fabric of the city itself. This course will be taught at NYU Shanghai and will count as an Away J-Term course.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
This is an Away course in Shanghai

title: Re-Inventions of Love
description: Engaging theater as an inherently interdisciplinary and innovative art form, this class proposes the investigation of love and art as a means to develop a richer understanding of what it is to be human. The course explores how the mythology, poetics, imagery, and emotion associated with romantic love have varied dramatically over time and in different cultures. Spanning several millennia and continents, our material will challenge us to look at gender, biology, identity, and faith as potent guides in reconciling our limitless potential for love and our inherent humanity. We will work with ancient texts like the Ramayana and the Upanishads, the poetry of Rumi and Lorca, theatrical works by Zeami, Shakespeare, and Sarah Kane, the music of Björk, Patti Smith, Sevdaliza, Anohni, FKA Twigs, and Radiohead, the photography of Cindy Sherman, the paintings of Frida Kahlo and the films of David Lynch—as well as a range of other artists. Responding to artistic distillations of this rich subject with embodied imagination and curiosity, we will create our own authentic artistic articulations and inventions, employing a range of artistic forms.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Contextual Innovation in Society
description: Why do innovations often differ across contexts? What are the elements of societies that shape and morph innovations? Does a society seed the innovation, or do innovations originate externally and independently from the context they grow into? This course will help students define and explore "contextual innovation”: how the bi-directional relationship between context and innovation can fundamentally determine its impact. Undertaking practical fieldwork in Abu Dhabi, students will leverage the city’s unique cultures to generate, design and pitch empathetic, culturally-competent, and context-specific innovations across industries and fields with a specific focus on transportation and medicine. Readings will include theoretical approaches from design and engineering, sociology, and anthropology. Case studies will include historical examples such as cars and airplanes, as well as contemporary examples including medicines and Uber. By the end of this course, students will have co-developed a framework for empathetic, contextual innovation translatable to other projects in their careers.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: On the Road Again: The Causes and Consequences of Domestic Migration
description: When we think about migration, it is usually in an international context. But in geographically vast nations like the United States, millions of citizens have moved and continue to move within national borders. Whether motivated by economic challenges, racial/ethnic discrimination or expulsion, or other factors, this sorting of humans has tremendous ramifications for the political, social, and economic fabric of communities - both at origin and destination. In this course, we will explore these consequences through two major domestic migration episodes in American history: the Trail of Tears and the Dust Bowl. Both profoundly shaped America in general and Oklahoma in particular, with the former leading to the forced resettlement of Native Americans to Oklahoma and the latter causing Oklahoma to lose hundreds of thousands of residents due to natural disasters. We will study these events through narrative accounts, history, literature, and music, leveraging Tulsa’s network of museums documenting their societal impact. Throughout the course, students will use our study of these migrations to explore the ramifications of contemporary geographic sorting in America and beyond. This course will be taught at NYU Tulsa and will count as an Away J-Term course.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
Class Times are shown in the Tulsa, USA time zone. Make sure you convert to your local time zone, if needed.
This is an Away course in Tulsa.

title: Maritime Archaeology of the Arabian Gulf and Western Indian Ocean
description: What does it mean to become maritime? How have oceans and seafaring shaped the ways people, ideas, and cultures have converged across time and space? This course investigates the UAE’s ocean history and early global connectivity through the maritime archaeological lens. In 2500 BCE, Magan ships crossing the Gulf opened vast networks to create global societies. By 750 CE, the maritime landscape of the Islamic world spanned the Atlantic, Mediterranean, and Indian Ocean worlds, from Al-Andalus to the Tarim Basin, and south to Sofala. We explore how maritime history from the Bronze Age to the present shaped the modern world and investigate how becoming maritime catalyzed and facilitated many social changes. We study how Arabian seafarers spread ideas, religions, technologies, and goods, shaping global identities made possible by connectivity. Through fieldwork in Abu Dhabi, we will learn celestial navigation and analyze ancient navigational texts to reflect on how sailors cognized the seas and coasts around them. Finally, using maritime archaeological methodologies, we will document ship structures to understand five millennia of the technologies that made a globalized world possible. Students should know how to swim (2 days of pool training).

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
Students should know how to swim (2 days of pool training).

title: Tango: Art, History, and Physics
description: How can dance both reflect and redefine national culture? What are the physical principles underlying a dance? This interdisciplinary course on tango explores both its artistic and political sides, paying special attention to the role audio-visual technologies have played in our understanding of its history. We trace its roots in the port cities of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, its fusion of African, European, and local influences, and its growth into a global symbol of national identity. We examine tango’s shifting political status--from cultural opposition to Argentine national emblem-- and its global reach through music, cinema, and performance. In tandem, we study analytically and physically the principles embedded in tango’s movement (balance, parsimony, and coordination); experiment with a virtual choreographic robot; and offer students the chance to dance. Fieldwork includes visits to a professional tango show, a tango dance hall, and museum; interviews with dancers; and hands-on tango instruction leading to student-created choreographies performed to music by a robot, as well as to short dance sequences performed by partners (no-touch optional). By creating both human and robotic choreography from a simple vocabulary, students gain insight into the relationships among history, improvisation and aesthetics. This course will be taught at NYU Buenos Aires and will count as an Away J-Term course.

title: Rupture and Repair: How to Lead Wisely in the Midst of Disagreement and Conflict
description: How do we navigate polarized perspectives and ideologies in today’s world without compromising our own? How can we sustain a better quality of disagreement across divides rather than cycles of revenge and retaliation? Centered on the lived experiences of conflict and sustainable peace, this course explores how to live and lead wisely amidst disagreement, with attention to the role of story, memory, power, and identity. Drawing from conflict transformation, peacebuilding, interfaith dialogue, and trauma-informed practice, the course blends classroom learning with dialogue groups, simulations, and fieldwork in polarized communities, turning conflict into collaboration. Students will use tools like the PIN Tool, Polarities, and Photovoice to map and transform conflict, wrestling with how to build a better quality of disagreement while focusing on what makes us different rather than shared commonalities. For the final project, students will design a collaborative action to repair the world and themselves. Living in an 800-year-old castle on the border between England and Scotland near Hadrian’s Wall, students learn from the site’s role in centuries of repairing rupture. This is an Away course taking place in the United Kingdom.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
This is an Away course in the United Kingdom

title: Empathy
description: What is empathy? Is it a universal capacity or culturally conditioned? (Is it comparable, for example, to "compassion" or "sympathetic joy" in Buddhist practice?) Can empathy be taught? Socially engineered? Does it make you a better student or citizen? What is empathetic design? Can AI empathize? Does or should empathy have limits? Drawing on scientific, social scientific, and humanistic disciplines and comparative cultural traditions and historical situations, this Colloquium allows students to examine the components and outcomes of NYUAD's own academic programs, including the Core. Can universities like ours confront global challenges without actively fostering an empathetic imagination? Can curricular design really change the world? Should faculty have more empathy for students' experience - and what would that mean? Do the arts make us more empathetic? When might empathy devolve into condescension or "othering"? Why have far-right political actors taken to attacking empathy as "toxic"? These and other questions will be addressed through readings, classroom exercises, and fieldwork, culminating in individual student manifestoes and collaborative podcast conversations.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Singing Revolution
description: This course explores singing as a powerful medium for engaging with histories of decolonization, revolution and feminism. Focusing on the politics of song and contribution of female vocalists, we examine the cross-cultural significance of four iconic singers, Umm Kulthum, Fairuz, Asmahan and Warda al-Jazairia. We investigate how these artists shaped modern Arab identities and diasporic understandings of belonging, particularly within the historical context of the British Empire and its metropole. From Asmahan’s alleged involvement in British espionage, to Fairuz’s performances at the Royal Albert Hall, to West End musicals about Umm Kulthum and Asmahan, London is a living archive of Arab cultural memory. Through academic inquiry, critical self-reflection and performance-based exploration at concerts, theatres and participatory workshops, students expand their investigation across wider geographies to ask: how and why does song transcend time and space to leave a lasting global impact? Building on this, students will curate a program of vocal works exploring the political role of song and its power as a tool for communication, propaganda, resistance, and social change.

title: The City and the Writer - Florence
description: How do cities shape the stories we tell, the languages we speak, and the forms our writing takes? How has literature reimagined urban space and transformed our understanding of identity, memory, and belonging? This course invites students to produce new creative works - poems, visual essays, short stories, plays, or films - inspired by Florence. Through readings, workshops, and field explorations, students will examine urban life across disciplines and borders, tracing journeys through real and imagined spaces while engaging questions of migration, culture, translation, and place. Students will have the unique opportunity to meet numerous residents of Florence, from theater makers, designers, architects, artists, filmmakers, feminists, actors, comedians and chefs.

title: Power, Identity, and the Real WWW (What Went Wrong?)
description: What is power, where does it come from, and why does it matter? What makes an identity, and why do some identities ignite conflict while others fade quietly? This course explores the dual forces of power and identity that shape the contemporary world, approaching these questions conceptually, historically, and practically. Students will engage with foundational debates on how to define and measure power, why identities emerge or dissolve, and how both dynamics drive cooperation, conflict, and creativity across the globe. From Bismarck to Putin, from civil rights movements to MAGA, from Rwanda’s reconciliation process to Hindu nationalism, from nations without states (Kurds, Tibetans) to states without cohesive nations (U.S., Canada, African multi-tribal states, Latin America), the course uses a diverse set of case studies as laboratories for exploring bigger ideas. This course combines classroom work with visits in Washington DC to think tanks, political lobbies, museums, and institutions where power and identity are debated, displayed, and contested. Students will leave with new conceptual tools for analyzing a rapidly shifting world and imagining their own place within it.

sections.notes:

title: Citizenship, Migration and Belonging
description: What is it to be and become a citizen, what does citizenship mean, and how does it impact our ways of being in the world? With roots in Ancient Greece and Rome, citizenship today defines the legal relationship between citizen and state. But discourse surrounding citizenship goes beyond the legalities to include collective identity and community solidarity. In this course, we will examine how citizenship is organized, performed, and contested in various contexts and at multiple levels of social organization - individual, familial, and societal. Using Florence, Italy, as our base, we will explore the origins and evolutions of citizenship from city-state to nation-state to supra-national status and beyond. We will also trace the intersections of race, gender, class, sexuality, age, and family with definitions of citizenship and access to citizenship across time and space. Fieldwork across Florence’s historic hubs of civic and political life, UNICEF research centers and migrant welcome centers will allow us to understand the ever-changing process of being and becoming citizens.

title: Unmediated
description: When every waking and resting moment of daily life is filtered through a screen, what remains of our "unmediated" selves? Is direct connection to environment and community still possible, or have we outsourced our identities and cognition to the cloud, like characters in dystopian films or fictions who cannot feel the weight of experiences that fall outside a technologically managed world? This course invites students to step outside our technological world to live as much as possible without digital technology. Free from phones, laptops and other digital devices, we examine how technology can mediate the self, manipulate our desires, and lead us to view the self as an object to be measured and optimized. Fieldwork in Abu Dhabi takes us trekking the UAE terrain with no digital aids and understanding the physiological impact of tech-free living. Finally, as we prepare to re-enter the technological world, we ask whether technology has a goal of its own—a telos—at odds with our own, what balance to strike between slow, unmediated living and a reactive, mediated life, and how to maintain this balance. This course involves hiking. Students must be without phones/computers for 2 weeks.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Cities Within the City: Visibility and Erasure in Buenos Aires
description: Urban life rests upon acts of seeing and unseeing; on what and whom we choose to notice, ignore, or erase. How do cities organize our attention, our gaze - in short, our relations and being - - into regimes of power, and how can ordinary citizens, artists, and activists reclaim who gets to be seen? Our exploration of these questions centers on Buenos Aires, a city shaped by powerful narratives of whiteness, progress, and modernity that have long obscured other presences and pasts. The course focuses on four key arenas: the city’s Afro-Argentine and Indigenous past and present; the struggles of memory activism during and after the last dictatorship; LGBTQ visibility; and class segregation. Students will participate in a range of field activities, including research visits to neighborhoods, museums, memory sites, and artists’ workshops, where they will observe the interplay between visibility and invisibility, interview guides and staff, and converse with artists and scholars. The course invites students to reflect on how cities render certain spaces and inhabitants invisible, and encourages them to imagine more inclusive ways of seeing and living together.

title: Scandinavian Safety and Security: How to ‘Hygge’ in a VUCA World
description: How do small, high-trust societies survive in an increasingly volatile world? Long ranked among the world's happiest and safest nations, Denmark balances a robust social welfare state with global innovation and helps build relations across cultural, religious, and political divides. A rising VUCA (Volatile, Uncertain, Complex, Ambiguous) landscape, marked by geopolitical shocks from the US and Russia, strains this domestic stability. Can the cultural concept of hygge - the conscious creation of cozy, comforting moments - explain how communities build trust and resilience, or does a turbulent era demand a new approach to human security building on past successes of the welfare state? Using Denmark as a living classroom, students connect political thinking, historical perspectives and contemporary debates to frontline defense and crisis management. Fieldwork and reflective assignments develop a practical framework for analyzing how small democratic states safeguard borders, infrastructure and social cohesion without sacrificing openness and trust. This is an away course in Denmark.

sections.notes:

This is an Away course in Denmark.

title: The Edge of Livability: Designing Cities for a Climate-Challenged Future
description: How should rapidly growing societies design, govern, and inhabit coastal cities under intensifying climatic extremes, so that they remain livable, equitable, and ecologically functional? This course uses the UAE as a case study for examining the defining challenge of the 21st century: how rapid urbanization can proceed in places already shaped by environmental constraints. Throughout Abu Dhabi and the wider Emirates, students examine the high-stakes balance between development, ecological limits, infrastructure demands, and climate risk. Targeted seminars are interwoven with guided fieldwork, including natural and urbanized site visits across coastal, terrestrial, and marine settings; inspections of major infrastructure projects; introductory environmental impact assessment (EIA) site surveys; and engagements with local experts and diverse stakeholders. These experiences enable a balanced appraisal of the constraints and opportunities that shape urbanization under challenging environmental conditions. By integrating ecology, urban metabolism, design, and policy, the course develops transferable insights into the future of cities in a warming world.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Information Design: Berlin as Data
description: What can we learn about a city, and what stories can we tell from the data it makes public? Berlin is one of Europe's most data-rich cities—its history, migration, infrastructure, and urban transformation are extensively documented. Using the living city as subject and inspiration, this course immerses students in transforming data into clear, compelling visual narratives. Class sessions cover visualization principles, geospatial mapping, and narrative structure using AI tools and industry-standard software. Daily warm-up exercises draw on Berlin, EU and global open datasets—building visual fluency and judgment. Students move between datasets and lived urban form, learning how data becomes legible—and how it can reveal, obscure, simplify, or distort reality. The final project is an original data-driven narrative about Berlin's neighborhoods, histories, economic or social trends. Ultimately, the course trains students to treat data as raw material and craft sound, targeted data-driven narratives. This is an away course in Berlin.

title: Bringing Imagination to Life: Immersive Worlds & Experiential Entertainment
description: In an era of digital saturation, why are we flocking to physical theme parks, mega-concerts, and "pop-up" worlds at record rates, and how does the global entertainment industry continue to up the game and evolve experiential entertainment into a cultural force? Using the Disney model of immersive storytelling, placemaking, and operational excellence as a framework, we will audit the machinery of enchantment to understand how theme parks transform media into high-stakes destinations that create shared meaning and economic value. Through case studies and fieldwork in Abu Dhabi, one of the world’s fastest-growing entertainment hubs, we will investigate the logistical, ethical, and psychological architecture of entertainment destination spaces and interview experts from experience designers and engineers to hospitality staff and data collectors of consumer sentiment. Students will analyze how these environments are financed and marketed, who they benefit or exclude, and how they drive tourism and diversify global economies. Ultimately, the course invites students to rethink “fun” itself: as a business strategy, a cultural language, and a powerful engine of human connection.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: AI: Emergence or Emergency?
description: Questions about whether AI represents a fundamental shift in the human trajectory, a transient phenomenon, or an existential threat animate public debate as automated tools remake daily life. What often goes missing is the broader history of science in which AI is embedded as well as new perspectives on science and technology that emerge when we foreground the intellectual labor of the Gulf. How is the UAE remaking AI, and how is AI remaking the UAE? In this course, blending academic inquiry, practical coding, and fieldwork, students investigate Abu Dhabi's active role in global AI innovation. They compare AI's modes of reasoning with cultural practices of human inquiry across the Hellenistic era, Islamic Golden Age, and Scientific Revolution. Students learn machine learning, neural networks, deep learning, unsupervised and reinforcement learning, and large language models, exploring practical applications in UAE healthcare, public administration, science, and education. Direct encounters with regulatory authorities promoting responsible AI complement discussions on societal impact, culminating in a fieldwork-based debate on the UAE’s role in developing and governing AI.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Harnessing the Power of Video Games for Cultural and Social Impact
description: Can video games improve lives and change the world? The $200 billion video game industry is larger than the film and music business with 3 billion gamers generating billions of ‘lean-forward’ hours of engagement every week. The medium has unique potential to foster cultural and social impact because video games are interactive and participatory. Games enable players to step into diverse roles, confront challenges, make choices, get feedback, and fail safely. They give players agency – the ability to make a difference in the game and ‘real’ world. Students will play and analyze games that have cultural and social impact goals, meet with local gaming studios and organizations, and research and develop a proposed Emirati culture game highlighting Emirati National Identity Values. Specific case studies such as the BAFTA-winning Never Alone will be reviewed; topics covered will range from aligning core game mechanics with cultural objectives to understanding the business and market dynamics for funding, developing, and releasing social impact games. Students will present their pitch for an Emirati culture game before a board of cultural and industry experts.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Listening to the Mangroves
description: What does the environment say through sound? Are we equipped to listen? This course acoustically investigates the health of one of the most valuable and threatened coastal ecosystems on Earth, Abu Dhabi’s mangroves. Hearing is immersive, three-dimensional, and continuous, and this makes listening a powerful tool to understand environments, relationships, places, and histories that vision alone cannot provide. Through fieldwork consisting of recording sessions in the mangroves of Abu Dhabi, complemented by a hands-on lab with the Sounding the Mangroves project research team, students will build a comprehensive sound map of the mangroves’ health. As part of this work, students will get a primer on the fundamental concepts of acoustic ecology, soundscape analysis, and ecoacoustics; learn to operate professional sound equipment; and interview research teams from Environment Agency Abu Dhabi (EAD) in the areas of Jubail and Al Mirfa. Becoming acoustemologists, or scholars of sound, students will gain a greater understanding of sound as a fundamental component of human and natural wellbeing, and of listening as a mode of ecological knowledge.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Belle Epoque Paris: An Urban Quilt of Literature, Music, Art, and Architecture
description: An Urban Quilt of Literature, Music, Art, and Architecture: "Life imitates art far more than art imitates life," wrote Oscar Wilde in his 1899 essay "The Decay of Lying: an Observation." What effect does art have in society? Can it open new ways of seeing, make us question our beliefs, reveal uncomfortable truths? Can it change the world? Or does it merely reflect prevailing power structures? And how should we make sense of the patriarchal and colonial perspectives common among artists from the past, even those most critical of their time? Students will explore Paris as an intertextual urban space, where the creative genius of 19th- and 20th-century artists reverberates throughout the city. We study fiction, poetry, painting, music, theater, opera, and film, focusing on literary works by Zola, Balzac, Colette, and Proust, and artworks by the impressionists, fauvists, pointillists, and cubists. Through interviews, research, and project-based visits to theaters, cafes, monuments, and museums, we will build a collective mindmap to make sense of the contradictions and intersections of Paris's urban space. Beyond learning about the past of a single city, we will seek to become critical navigators of the present and future. This is an away course in Paris.

sections.notes:

Class Times are shown in the Paris, France time zone. Make sure you convert to your local time zone, if needed.
This is an Away course in Paris.

title: Cosmopolis
description: Cosmopolis examines contemporary cosmopolitanism—its promises, limits, and critics—through Abu Dhabi as a living city within the UAE: a place that has staked its global ambitions on plurality while navigating the tensions that often arise around issues such as security, governance, migration, heritage, and culture. How is Abu Dhabi redefining cosmopolitanism? How does society function in a city built for the world? How do design, narratives, public space, law and policy shape who feels at home—and who does not? Students connect moral and political theory to on-the-ground experience through site visits to public and civic spaces, practicing rapid ethnographic methods to map where pluralism thrives and where it strains. Ethnographic fieldwork and two short writing reflections on themes of heritage, culture, religion, social initiatives, and education build analytical skills throughout the course; a final team project proposes a practical intervention to foster civic life. By the end, students can evaluate cosmopolitan ideas and design proposals grounded in field evidence and thus track how debates over cosmopolitanism shape the UAE’s and even the world’s joint futures.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: The Business of Attention
description: What will command human attention in the future, and who will control it? In an era of infinite content, algorithmic feeds, AI-generated media, and constant digital distraction, attention has become one of our most valuable, contested resources. This course examines how entertainment, media, technology, sports, advertising, and social platforms compete to capture, shape, and monetize human attention. Drawing from business, psychology, and cultural studies, we explore how audiences discover and assign meaning to content in a fragmented marketplace. Through fieldwork in Abu Dhabi, students will study how algorithms shape culture and taste, and how societies balance global media influences with local traditions, and why some stories, brands, and creators break through while others struggle to be seen. Examining examples from global sports leagues, social media creators, and gaming to emerging cultural institutions across the Gulf, we ask: in a world of infinite choice, what continues to earn human attention and trust? If we are what we pay attention to, attention may be the defining currency of modern life, shaping how we understand ourselves and the future.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Sports Psychology: Fields, Fandoms, Communities
description: How does sport shape who we are, where we belong, and the ways we build community? Abu Dhabi has emerged as a model of sports-led development, investing in infrastructure, events, and partnerships that advance economic diversification and social transformation. As the emirate transitions from hosting events that attract fans to creating experiences that connect people, sport takes on new meaning in daily life. This course explores how sports cultures take root, grow, and bring people together in ways that result in changed lives. Grounded in the local sports scene while giving attention to global contexts, the course examines the physical, psychological, and social dimensions of human engagement with sport. Through fieldwork across sports facilities and training grounds, students analyze how participation and fandom shape identity, belonging, and wellbeing. Learning interlaces current events, historical examples, industry case studies, behavioral theories, and management principles across business, government, and non-profit sectors that can be applied to understanding the role of the individual in building a functioning society.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Pandemics and Plagues
description: Throughout recorded history, pandemics and plagues have occupied an outsized significance in human culture. How are pandemics shaped by the intersections of pathogens, people, and place? What do plagues reveal about the fault lines and fractures in society? Can lessons from past pandemics – especially our recent experience with COVID-19 – help us better prepare for the next outbreak? Using global literature and film, we explore how people have narrated, interpreted, and imagined infectious diseases through time and across continents. Case studies include the Black Death, tuberculosis, cholera, the Spanish flu, HIV/AIDS, and COVID-19. Fieldwork with medical centers, public health resources, and disease-monitoring data initiatives in Abu Dhabi brings our study of pandemics into the present day by providing first-hand insights into the scope, monitoring, and prevention of infectious diseases.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Futurism and Art
description: What happens when a state makes futurism a core priority? And how can artists, curators, and developers engage with this agenda, by speculating alternatives for a future worth living and building? This course examines how intellectuals and state officials have approached the idea of the future in the past and in the present. What were the political stakes of modernization theories and oppositional movements, such as Italian Futurism, Bolshevism, Afrofuturism, and Arab Futurism? And what can these histories tell us about Gulf/UAE futurism as both an aesthetic and a political project? Using the UAE's cultural and economic sectors as examples, we explore how the future of the UAE and its region is being imagined and constructed at arts institutions, such as the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, Sharjah Art Foundation, and Diriyah Art Futures in Riyadh, and through the connections of the art world to real estate developers, oil companies, and AI. By researching these institutions’ language and aesthetics and co-designing and curating a group exhibition as the final project, students learn how art can transform the imagination into a space of active resistance and defiance against despair.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: English
description: Who does English belong to, and in a globalized society, does the concept of "native speaker" still hold meaning? This course examines the shifting boundaries of language ownership and identity in a globalized world. We will analyze the unseen power of English as both a tool for commerce and digital exchange and as a site of struggle over who defines the language. By exploring English as a Lingua Franca (ELF), we contrast traditional notions of linguistic "correctness" with how English is actually used by more than a billion speakers worldwide. We will investigate how educational policies, assessments, and classroom practices often uphold rigid standards that marginalize certain varieties of English as well as local and home languages, in addition to the role of AI in shaping global English and whether it empowers multilingual speakers or marginalizes those outside the "standard." Students will reflect on how their identities and opportunities are shaped by the perceived "nativeness" of their speech. Fieldwork in Abu Dhabi’s high-stakes, multilingual ELF context allows students to analyze how diverse communities reclaim and reshape English to suit their own needs.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Sound, Voice, and Place in the Age of AI
description: What does it mean for a place to have a "sound," and how do geography, migration, and community shape a local musical identity block by block? How have technologies of capture and reproduction, from the 78 rpm disc to generative AI, changed who gets to make music, and who gets credit for it? As AI becomes capable of generating convincing music and voices, what remains irreducibly human about music? Every city has a sound, but few offer students the chance to make music inside it. This intensive, studio-based course uses Tulsa, home to Western swing, singer-songwriter Americana, gospel, jazz, and hip-hop, as both subject and workshop. Students spend most of their time composing, recording, and performing original work alongside two lead instructors: a multi-platinum producer and mixer, and a Tulsa-based songwriter, multi-instrumentalist, and vocalist for Hanson and Tinted Window. Classroom study on the neuroscience of music alongside encounters with Tulsa's musicians, venues, and traditions, including its Americana heritage and legacy of Black musicians, culminate in an original body of recorded work each student will write, perform, and produce.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
Class Times are shown in the Tulsa, USA time zone. Make sure you convert to your local time zone, if needed.
This is an Away course in Tulsa

title: Architecture and Landscape Design for an Uncertain Future
description: How do we design for an uncertain future? How can design respond to the climate crisis in ways that mitigate impacts of the built environment? What are potential tradeoffs and unintended consequences of designing during the energy transition? Using Abu Dhabi as a practical lens, this course explores architectural and landscape sustainability, a method using design to respond to climate’s environmental impacts and strengthen community wellbeing. Students investigate the philosophical roots of environmentalism, navigate regional climate challenges, and cultivate design thinking skills through resilient technologies and AI performance modeling. Fieldwork visits to Masdar City, Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, and Abu Dhabi Sustainability Week 2027 allow students to examine different visions of sustainability in practice and explore the values and interests they serve. Through daily design exercises, students integrate fieldwork and multiple perspectives on sustainable and resiliency principles with design. As a final project, students create an applied campus project for NYUAD, presenting their sustainable solutions to a faculty jury.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Bitter and Sweet: The Business of Chocolate
description: The cocoa industry today serves as a microcosm of the global economy and faces considerable ecological, economic, social and cultural challenges that need addressing on a global scale. Students will study the world of chocolate over its entire value chain, exploring its history and culture, cultivation and economic development, business and economics, marketing and branding, politics and trade, science and nutrition, sustainability and labor issues as well as the future of the industry amidst climate and development challenges. Why is one of the world's most beloved foods - chocolate - built on a foundation of systemic inequities, and how can industry multinationals address this imbalance? Students will engage in interviews with local stakeholders and directly experience chocolate through workshops and tastings to explore the unique challenges and opportunities that this important industry faces in Ghana. Insights derived from this course will be relevant not only to the chocolate industry, but also to others that grapple with similar issues on a global scale. This is an away course in Accra.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
Class Times are shown in the Accra, Ghana time zone. Make sure you convert to your local time zone, if needed.
This is an Away course in Accra.

title: Politics of Culture: Ethnographic Fieldwork in the UAE
description: What is the role of culture in political life? Why do modern states organize all aspects of daily life from holidays and public rituals to citizens’ language, dress, leisure, and social comportment? How does culture legitimize political power? This colloquium examines the relationship between politics and culture through ethnographic fieldwork. Students will read primary texts on ethnographic methods and on cultural theories of power, while utilizing Abu Dhabi’s vibrant cultural institutions, public spaces, and community settings to practice fieldwork techniques. In these sites, students will conduct participant observation and interviews, take field notes, and produce reflective writing. Class seminars will tie together the readings, discussions, and hands-on fieldwork experience. Drawing on their ethnographic research, students will develop an original analysis of how cultural symbols reinforce the state’s political vision in the UAE and beyond.

sections.notes: Requires Department Consent

title: Contemporary Art Jewelry
description: Why is jewelry such a powerful means of expression in today's globalized world? Why have humans across virtually every culture developed the practice of adorning themselves with jewelry? Through cultural and artistic lenses, students examine jewelry in its broadest significance, with particular emphasis on contemporary art jewelry as a form of communication. The course begins with an anthropological inquiry into human self-adornment, investigating decoration practices across cultures as vehicles for identity and expression, before shifting to the UAE context and the rich history of pearl diving. Working with an internationally recognized contemporary jeweler, students will explore the relationship between jewelry, light, and reflection as vehicles for meaning, experimenting with materials to develop concepts into a wearable piece. Fieldwork across the Abu Dhabi Gold Souk and Sheikh Zayed National Museum will allow students to explore the cultural narratives jewelry embodies in the UAE and beyond. Finally, students present their work in an exhibition at the Arts Center Cube, showcasing jewelry’s rich intersection with art, culture, economics, and personal expression.
