title: Making the Desert Home: The Archaeology of Al Ain Oasis
description: The Archaeology of Al Ain Oasis: How do societies make an arid environment habitable, and what does archaeology tell us about the ancient origins of the UAE's thriving economy? This course investigates how communities in Al Ain have created, maintained, and reimagined oasis life over five millennia. Focusing on the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Al Ain and its ancient system of falaj underground aqueducts, students will consider whether oases are best understood as engineered environments, ecological systems, economic enterprises, cultural landscapes, or a blend of each. Students will undertake an archaeological survey as part of the Al Ain Oasis Mapping Project, examining how water technology, agricultural practices, trade opportunities, labour availability, and political organisation shaped the landscape. The course will combine morning fieldwork in the oasis with afternoon seminars and site visits, exploring theoretical perspectives in archaeology and case studies in cultural heritage management. Creating an archaeological map of the oasis as a final product, students will contribute directly to documenting Emirati heritage while developing evidence-based perspectives on how desert environments become - and remain - home. This is a fully off-campus fieldwork intensive course. Students will stay in Al-Ain for two weeks with a day off in Abu Dhabi on the weekend. They will work outside in the heat/dust so practical clothing, sturdy shoes, sunhats, sunglasses, water bottles, etc., are essential. Students should dress in respectful clothing while in Al-Ain. Abayas are unsuited to archaeological fieldwork, and students have opted to wear a lab coat. This course counts as an Abu Dhabi based course.

title: What It Costs Us to Win: Lessons on Success from Athletics
description: Lessons on success from athletics: What does it mean to win, to succeed? Who defines winning, what are the costs, and why does it matter? Can you achieve a "win" and still "lose"? In athletics, answers are clear: points, trophies, records, and awards. However, these questions also show up in life: in school, parenting, career, and relationships, we desire to "win" and be seen as "winners" at whatever we do. In this course, we use athletics to explore the parallels and pitfalls of success on the field of play and in life, with particular attention to success trajectories in the UAE and how the emerging sports scene is redefining what it means to win. We discuss how cultural values and political ideologies shape how we define and approach success and the costs and benefits for individuals and societies. Students will learn from the most "successful" coaches, athletes, and scholars of human development. We prioritize learning from athletic dynasties that show how success rooted in care, collaboration, commitment, and contentment - counterintuitive to success driven by individualism, dominance, and competition - offers a blueprint not only for building winning individuals but also for a more just and humane society.

title: The Science of Smell
description: Of all our senses, why is smell the most neglected yet the most emotionally explosive? Is scent a mere luxury, or is it the primary architect of our memories, social boundaries, and cultural identities? This interactive, discussion-based course explores the chemistry behind our sense of smell and its emotional, cultural, and psychological impact. The course makes immediate the invisible molecules of scent around us by examining the molecular basis of smell, olfactory biology, perfume composition, and scent’s role in memory, culture, identity, and politics. Students will map the topography of everyday scents and trade routes across the UAE, decode perfume structures, and even create their own fragrances. No prior science background required—just a curious nose and an open mind.

title: Europe Between Washington and Moscow: Can Western Values Survive?
description: Europe is not just a continent; it is a thousand-year-old culture, a political project, a set of moral ideals. Modern Europe was founded on a belief in individual liberty and social equality, the rule of law, reason and secularism. That ethos is now endangered by, among other things, an increasingly belligerent Russia and an illiberal America. This colloquium will ask how, and whether, Europe can preserve its identity and values amid these grave challenges. Through visits to cathedrals, palaces, museums, libraries, concert halls, and memorials treating Prague as one of our main texts, and through readings and discussion, students will examine how Europe has been shaped by art and philosophy, by empire and religion, by nationalism, communism and democracy. We will then move on to the contemporary struggle over the survival of this project, focusing on the war in Ukraine, the rise of right-wing populism, immigration, and deteriorating relations with Washington, which has compelled Europeans to recognize that they can no longer count on protection from across the ocean. Students will engage firsthand with journalists, security analysts, and policy scholars shaping contemporary Europe.

title: The New Silk Roads: China, the UAE, and the Making of Globalization
description: How do China and the United Arab Emirates shape each other, and how do ordinary people experience their political, economic, cultural, and social connections to make globalization? This course examines the historical and contemporary realities of China–UAE ties and the making of new silk roads. Moving beyond Western narratives, we approach China and the Gulf as participants in a dynamic South–South exchange shaped by trade, migration, religion, language, education, and state-led development. Students will study the long history of interaction between China and the Arab and Islamic worlds and the Gulf's evolving position in global networks as the foundation for analyzing recent developments, including China’s economic expansion, the Belt and Road Initiative, and Chinese migration to the UAE. Fieldwork across diasporic markets, Chinese-language schools, and mosques reveals how globalization is not solely driven by states or corporations, but produced by migrants, merchants, teachers, religious leaders, consumers, and families. Completing a final digital ethnography, students will analyze globalization as a lived and contested reality shaped through everyday intercultural encounters.

title: Connection by Design: Can AI Strengthen Human Connection?
description: We are facing a global crisis of connection, reflected in the rising levels of depression, loneliness, partisan divides, suicide, and violence. While technology is often blamed, there is a growing consensus that the problem is not technology but the way it is designed with a wide variety of design features that inevitably promote disconnection and isolation. How can digital technology and AI be designed to deepen human-to-human connection? Drawing on the science of human connection, this course examines the skills that enable human to human connection and bridge divides, and has students work in pairs to develop research grounded proposals for Connection-by-Design technology that strengthens human relationships rather than disconnecting them. The UAE will serve as the first country to offer such opportunities within a rapidly changing, technologically ambitious, and culturally diverse society. Students will learn and practice the skills necessary for human connection through interviews with local community members and apply this fieldwork to their UAE-specific product designs.

title: Body in Balance: Discovering Sleep, Nutrition, and Exercise
description: What does it mean to have a healthy body, and can we rehack our biology in a rapidly changing world? Who among us has not struggled to balance fatigue, eating well and exercise against competing pressures of work and personal life? This course explores the interconnected science of sleep, nutrition, and exercise, and the tension between fast-paced lives and healthy lifestyles. With the UAE a key player in global food and energy systems, we explore biological and ethical costs of our modern, high-stress life, considering how to break free from these cycles and live healthier lives. Our inquiry into who gets to live a healthy life tracks the UAE's transition from a lifestyle centered on physical labor, traditional whole-food diets, and natural sleep patterns to one characterized by sedentary work, ultra-processed foods, and artificial light, taking us into fieldwork in health clinics, food markets, historic communities, national museums, and UNESCO Heritage sites. Students conduct two caffeine timing experiments, maintain a sleep diary, exercise log, and food journal, carry out an Abu Dhabi food environment audit, and produce a cross-national comparative analysis of health behaviors.

title: Rebels, Punks, and Bohemians
description: This course about counterculture explores how the young and not-so-young reject mainstream society to embrace something wilder and more authentic, whether in art, music, literature, politics, or love. Can misfits and rebels bring about social change? What happens to society when today’s punks become tomorrow’s politicians, when anti-art winds up in a museum? Our setting for these questions is Madrid. We’ll tackle the subject genealogically, tracing countercultural movements back in time from the present day to the early 20th century. Starting with Spain’s “15-M” Occupy demonstrations in the 2010s, we’ll plunge into the punk explosion of the 1970s and 80s known as the Movida. We’ll then examine local echoes of the global 1960s, and finally look at the artistic ferment of the “Silver Age” of the 1910s and 20s. The goal is to understand the aesthetics of rebellion in its original context. In streets, plazas, museums, and bars, we’ll study Madrid’s countercultural spirit up close. As a final project, students will invent their own movement, complete with its own zine and style of clothing. This is an Away course in Madrid.

title: When Home is a Photograph: Vernacular Archives of the Arab World and Black Life
description: What insights about photography come to light when vernacular photographs from the Arab world and African American life are put in dialogue? How do archives of photographs create home and frameworks of belonging or omission? This course explores the rich photographic cultures represented in two archives: the Akkasah Photography Archive at NYU Abu Dhabi and the Peter J. Cohen Collection of Black life in NYC. Both archives feature vernacular photographs – those that capture everyday life through studio portraits, travel albums, identification photographs, and snapshots. A key component of the course is the hands-on engagement with these photographic objects, allowing students to explore their cultural significance as photographs and their status as objects to be physically held while centering questions of home. Students will culminate their studies by curating a photo exhibition as a final project. Engaging the vibrant photographic arts scene of the UAE, the course includes local speakers and field visits are planned to the Alserkal Avenue arts district, Gallery 421, the NYUAD Arts Center photography darkroom and the Akkasah Photography Archive.

title: Photography and Witnessing
description: What does it take to be a witness rather than look at events passively, without feeling compelled to respond? What are the ethical, political, cultural, legal and personal stakes in witnessing? Can photographic images turn us into witnesses and motivate us to respond to what we see, or do we have to witness an event personally to be moved to act? This seminar uses contemporary Berlin as a case study for how images are used (in memorials, museums and public life) to confront viewers with pictures so that they take responsibility for a shared but often contested future. Through the creation of image-based projects in small, rotating teams, students learn how images can either document or distort the past, compel us to action or numb us, and either be tools or obstacles for individuals or groups to be socially and politically recognized. Readings include key texts from the history and theory of photography, some texts on the political and social use of images, as well as important critical responses to iconic images.

title: Wealth and Inequality in the Global City
description: Wealth and Inequality in the Global City: The rapid increase in wealth and income inequality in many countries is concentrated in the world’s leading cities. What is driving the concentration of wealth, and what are its consequences? Using New York City as our laboratory, we will explore some of the ways in which wealth and power are created and maintained, as well as examining some of the social consequences of high levels of inequality for families and individuals who are being left behind. Readings and class discussions will explore the social and political economy of inequality in the work of contemporary social sciences. We will deepen our understanding of key issues through field trips, films, and conversations with key leaders in the world of finance and business, government, as well as NGOs working to alleviate some of the most serious consequences of poverty and inequality in New York. This is an Away course in New York.

title: Mediterranean Foodways
description: A bottle of olive oil, a basket of warm bread, platters of fresh produce, grilled fish: these are stock images of the Mediterranean diet. But whose Mediterranean, whose diet, and whose interests does this image serve? How does Mediterranean food relate to memory? How do Mediterranean foodways relate to forms of social difference, including ethnicity, gender, class, and nationality? How do Mediterranean foodways engage with the processes of globalization? What have been the effects of migration across the Mediterranean on its foodways? How do Mediterranean foodways respond to the pressures of climate change and industrial agriculture? In this class students will explore the intersections of food and culture through critical analysis of the Mediterranean diet and the Slow Food movement, and through field excursions to local food markets, an olive oil producer, and an experimental university food lab. Through case studies from around the Mediterranean as well as cooking and tasting, students will interrogate the multiple and contradictory ways traditions are created and recreated in a globalized world. This is an Away course in Florence.
